title: Mission: When Red Tide Crossed Into Miami’s Shark Refuge
text:
For most of the decade between 2009 and 2021, coastal sharks off Miami and Biscayne Bay lived in a natural geographic refuge from Florida’s red tide blooms. Combining standardized drumline surveys from the University of Miami (4,351 sets and 3,398 individual shark records) with Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) water monitoring reveals a stark divide across the peninsula: while Karenia brevis blooms (>= 10,000 cells/L) erupt almost annually along Southwest Florida’s Gulf coast, South Florida’s Atlantic coast (Longitude > -80.5°) recorded zero bloom samples in 11 out of 13 study years. Even so, mark-recapture tracks show that this boundary is permeable for large coastal predators—Tiger and Lemon sharks tagged off Miami (-80.1°) swam hundreds of kilometers around the Florida Keys directly into Gulf waters where blooms are frequent.









That geographic shelter broke down dramatically in 2018 (Panel A, dark red points). During the severe 2017–2018 Southwest Florida red tide crisis, Loop Current and Florida Current eddies carried Karenia brevis cells around the Florida Keys and up the Atlantic coast into Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach waters. Out of all 95 Atlantic-coast bloom samples recorded in South Florida across the entire 13-year FWC archive, 90 occurred in the autumn of 2018 alone, pushing overall South Florida bloom prevalence to a study-wide peak of 27.1% of all water samples (with concentrations exceeding 50 million cells/L).
At the same time, the University of Miami drumline survey recorded a clear dip in coastal shark catch rates, falling from 0.73–0.88 sharks per set during the low-bloom years of 2014–2017 down to 0.61 sharks per set in 2018 (Panel B). Because Karenia brevis neurotoxins (brevetoxins) cause massive fish kills and depleted dissolved oxygen in nearshore waters, mobile coastal sharks frequently move offshore or along the coast to avoid toxic blooms, while slower-moving benthic residents face higher exposure. Together, the spatial map, migration tracks, and annual catch record show why South Florida’s shark community cannot be treated as isolated from Gulf of Mexico harmful algal blooms: sharks cross between both coasts on their own, and in extreme bloom years, red tide crosses right over to them.

      🌊 The Big Question We're Investigating
      
        Along Southwest Florida's Gulf coast, microscopic algae called Karenia brevis bloom nearly every year,
        releasing neurotoxins and depleting oxygen in coastal waters. Meanwhile, South Florida's Atlantic coast around Miami
        and Biscayne Bay is usually sheltered—until rare ocean current events (like in 2018) carry red tide
        right around the Florida Keys!
      
      
        By combining 13 years of University of Miami shark drumline surveys with Florida FWC & NOAA
        red tide water monitoring, this website explores how sharks move between coasts and how their catch rates change during bloom years.

title: Sharks & Red Tide Correlation
text: To test how coastal shark catch rates relate to Karenia brevis harmful algal blooms, we join the University of Miami drumline survey (2009–2021) with Florida FWC red tide water samples across South Florida (24.4°N–27.0°N, -82.8°W to -79.8°W) by year and by month. Following FWC thresholds, a water sample is classified as an active red tide bloom when Karenia brevis concentrations reach >= 10,000 cells/L.

title: Sharks & Red Tide Correlation
text:
Annual & Monthly Correlation
Across the 13 survey years (2009–2021), mean sharks caught per drumline set and South Florida red tide bloom prevalence show a moderate negative correlation:

Annual Pearson correlation: \(r = -0.44\) (Spearman rank \(\rho = -0.37\), \(n = 13\) years)
Monthly Pearson correlation: \(r = -0.27\) (\(n = 115\) well-sampled months with at least 10 drumline sets and 10 water samples)










Years with heavier red tide activity—most notably 2018, when 27.1% of South Florida water samples reached bloom concentrations and red tide spilled onto the Atlantic coast—coincided with lower coastal shark catch rates (0.61 sharks per set). Conversely, low-bloom years such as 2009, 2010, 2014, and 2015 saw higher average catch rates (0.82–1.64 sharks per set).

Key Takeaways

Consistent Negative Association: Both annual (\(r = -0.44\)) and monthly (\(r = -0.27\)) aggregations show lower shark catch rates when regional red tide prevalence is higher.
Why the Correlation Is Moderate Rather Than Stronger: Most FWC blooms occur along Southwest Florida’s Gulf coast, whereas UM’s drumline sets are concentrated off Miami and the Florida Keys. Direct overlap happens primarily when Gulf blooms wrap around the Keys into Atlantic waters (as in autumn 2018) or when mobile coastal sharks migrate between Gulf and Atlantic waters.

title: About
text:
Data Sources
This project combines three publicly available marine and environmental datasets:

University of Miami Coastal Shark Surveys (2009–2021)
Standardized drumline survey records from Miami through the middle Florida Keys, encompassing 21,755 drumlines (4,351 sets) and 3,398 captured sharks across 15 species. Includes catch-per-set counts, environmental measurements, total length and sex records, and mark-recapture migration tracks. Published by Abigail Tinari and Neil Hammerschlag (2021), “An ecological assessment of large coastal shark communities in South Florida,” Ocean & Coastal Management (doi:10.1016/j.ocecoaman.2021.105772).
Florida FWC Red Tide Monitoring Database (2007–Present)
Coastal water sample records maintained by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) Fish and Wildlife Research Institute, reporting sample dates, geographic coordinates, water depth, and Karenia brevis cell concentrations (cells/L) across Florida waters.
NOAA HABSOS (Harmful Algal BloomS Observing System)
Historical Karenia brevis cell count observations and accompanying physical water measurements (temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen) across the Gulf of Mexico, archived by the National Centers for Environmental Information / NOAA HABSOS.
